title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership Predictably Unpredictable
author: Nickhart
summary: Nickhart examines a productive tension in school improvement: schools are complex adaptive systems with unpredictable outcomes, yet experienced leaders predict things (resistance, plateaus, compliance without commitment) with reasonable reliability. His resolution: complex systems have unpredictable outcomes but predictable emergent patterns of behaviour. The work is to recognise those patterns, not to predict specific outcomes. Three recurring patterns: push harder and something pushes back; new initiatives show early promise then settle into existing culture; address one issue and another emerges. School improvement plans are structurally ill-suited to this reality because they present linear cause-and-effect logic to satisfy governance requirements, and the danger comes when leaders begin to believe the plan. What looks like resistance is often rational adaptation -- teachers managing pressure and scarcity by interpreting mandates in locally sensible ways. Nickhart's prescription: better school improvement pattern recognition, planning for emergence rather than assuming direct cause and effect.
points: - Complex systems have unpredictable outcomes but predictable emergent patterns of behaviour; the task for school leaders is to develop better pattern recognition, not to predict specific results. - School improvement plans must present linear logic (goal, action, impact) to satisfy governance requirements -- the structural incentive is to believe a simplified model even when practitioners know reality is messier. - Three systems-thinking patterns repeat across schools: increased pressure produces compliance not deep change; new approaches show early promise then settle into existing culture; solving one visible problem causes another to emerge. - What looks like resistance to an initiative is often rational adaptation: teachers managing pressure and time scarcity by interpreting mandates in locally sensible ways -- which is exactly what complex systems do. - Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety offers a practical corrective: a single, tightly defined approach cannot absorb the variety of a complex school; improvement strategies must match the complexity of the context.
quotes: There is the nuance: complex systems are unpredictable in their outcomes but we could argue that there are predictable emergent patterns of behaviour. We cannot say with confidence what will happen but we can become better at recognising the patterns through which systems respond.

The problem is predictable: we design plans based on how we hope the system behaves, not how it actually behaves. Plans tend to assume a world in which cause and effect are relatively direct. Do this and you will get that.
It becomes a problem when we begin to believe it. While the plan may present a neat story of improvement, the system it is applied to is far less tidy.

When fidelity to an approach has not happened, people in the system might not be resisting improvement for the sake of it. They are making rational decisions based on the pressures and information available to them.

Cause and effect are not closely related in time and space. Actions taken now may have consequences that only become visible later and those consequences are shaped by everything that happens in between.

The harder you push, the harder the system pushes back. Increased pressure often produces behaviours that appear to align with expectations but do not necessarily reflect deeper change. Compliance rises and risk taking falls.
